overview.text: Bread is a baked food usually made from flour and water; recipes and shapes vary. Archaeologists have found charred bread-like crumbs at Shubayqa 1 in Jordan, dating to about 14,400 years ago—evidence that some hunter-gatherers made bread before farming became widespread. In ancient Egypt, bread was a staple, made mainly from emmer wheat in flat and conical forms, and bread rations could serve as payment. Bread also has religious significance: in the Catholic celebration of the Eucharist, bread and wine are understood by the Church to become the Body and Blood of Christ. These varied uses make bread both everyday nourishment and a culturally meaningful food.

key_facts.text: At Shubayqa 1 in Jordan, charred crumbs provide evidence of bread-making about 14,400 years ago, before settled agriculture.
The Shubayqa bread was likely an unleavened flatbread made from wild cereals and club-rush tubers.
In Middle Kingdom Egypt, bread was a dietary staple; emmer-wheat loaves came in shapes including flat and long conical forms.
Ancient Egyptian bread rations could be payment for workers and household staff.
In Catholic teaching, bread and wine in the Eucharist become the Body and Blood of Christ; this is a religious belief, not a claim about ordinary bread.
